unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply gowning and draping techniques that protect patient privacy and modesty during examinations and procedures.
- Assist patients into clinician-directed positions using safe transfer and positioning practices.
- Preserve patient dignity, comfort, and autonomy through respectful communication and consent-based assistance.
- Recognize fall risks and apply environmental, transfer, and escalation practices that keep patients safe.
- Follow scope-of-practice boundaries by escalating clinical and safety concerns to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A gown is like a curtain on a stage. It lets the doctor see only the part being checked while keeping the rest of the person covered and private.

### Question 2

You only take off as much as needed for the checkup, like rolling up one sleeve for a shot instead of taking off your whole shirt.

### Question 3

Think of it like a fitting room at a store. You leave the person alone to change, and you knock before coming back in.

### Question 4

If a friend is struggling with a zipper, you ask, 'Want me to help?' and only help if they say yes. It's the same idea here.

### Question 5

A gown is like a backward robe: the opening goes in the back and you tie it so it doesn't flap open.

### Question 6

If you don't want to wear a costume for a school play, a grown-up shouldn't force you. They listen and figure out another plan. Patients get the same respect.

### Question 7

When you know what's going to happen, a new experience feels less scary. Telling the patient the plan makes the checkup less frightening.

### Question 8

If a blanket is too small, you grab another one so everyone stays warm and covered. We do the same with gowns, kindly and without comment.

### Question 9

If the doctor only needs to check your arm, you roll up that sleeve and leave the rest of your clothes on.

### Question 10

You put on your swimsuit right before you swim, not when you first arrive at the pool. The gown goes on right before the part that needs it.

### Question 11

When you're chilly, someone hands you a warm blanket. We do the same for patients in thin gowns.

### Question 12

When you change clothes at home, you shut the door so no one sees. The exam room door or curtain works the same way.

### Question 13

For a checkup of the lower body, only the lower half is uncovered, and a sheet keeps it private until the doctor is ready.

### Question 14

If a friend's arm hurts, you help them take off their jacket slowly and carefully. We help patients the same gentle way.

### Question 15

The assistant is like a helper who offers a hand when getting dressed, but always lets the person decide what they want help with.

### Question 16

If someone has a special rule about what they wear, you listen and find a way that respects their rule and still gets the job done.

### Question 17

When you stand up after sitting a while, someone stays close in case you wobble, and they make sure your robe stays shut.

### Question 18

You use a clean towel after a shower, not someone else's used one. Each patient gets a clean gown for the same reason.

### Question 19

A drape is like a blanket that covers everything except the one spot the doctor needs to see.

### Question 20

It's like a magician revealing one card at a time instead of the whole deck. We show only the part being checked.

### Question 21

Like closing one book before opening the next, we cover the tummy before we uncover the legs.

### Question 22

Before a show starts, the curtain stays closed until everyone is ready. We keep the sheet over the patient until the doctor is ready.

### Question 23

Just like tucking someone in with a blanket, we cover the patient with a sheet to keep them cozy.

### Question 24

To check your back, you roll over while keeping the blanket on, then we pull it down just a little.

### Question 25

During a procedure, the assistant is like a stagehand who keeps the curtain where it should be so only the right part shows.

### Question 26

For a heart sticker test, we uncover just the spots for the stickers and keep everything else covered with a sheet.

### Question 27

A gown is something you wear; a drape is a cover that goes on top of you, like a blanket.

### Question 28

If you're waiting on the table, someone makes sure you're covered and not left alone in the dark.

### Question 29

When checking one leg, we keep the other leg and your top half under the blanket, like only sticking one foot out of the covers.

### Question 30

If someone is shivering, you offer them a blanket. We do the same and ask if they're comfortable.

### Question 31

The doctor is like the coach who calls the play; the assistant helps the player get into position.

### Question 32

Supine is like lying on your back looking up at the ceiling, like when you sleep on your back.

### Question 33

Prone is like lying on your tummy.

### Question 34

Fowler's is like sitting up in a recliner chair with your back supported.

### Question 35

It's like a recliner: semi-Fowler's is halfway back, and high Fowler's is almost sitting straight up.

### Question 36

Sims' is like lying on your left side with your top leg bent up toward your chest.

### Question 37

Lithotomy is like lying on your back with your knees bent and your feet resting on footrests.

### Question 38

Trendelenburg tilts the table like a slide, with the head down and feet up.

### Question 39

Getting onto a high bed is easier with a step stool, like using a step to reach a high shelf.

### Question 40

If someone needs help up a step, you offer your hand and steady them; you don't yank them up.

### Question 41

After helping someone sit, you make sure they're steady before you walk away.

### Question 42

You tilt a chair back slowly and tell the person, 'I'm tilting you up now,' so they aren't surprised.

### Question 43

You scoot to the edge of the bed before lying down so you don't end up too far over one side.

### Question 44

When you help someone roll over in bed, you brace them so they don't tip or strain.

### Question 45

If something hurts, you tell the grown-up in charge so they can fix it; you don't just say 'tough it out.'

### Question 46

Like writing down what happened in your diary right away so you don't forget, we write down how the patient was positioned.

### Question 47

Before starting, you ask, 'Are you comfy? Do you know what's happening next?' That's the caring thing to do.

### Question 48

Before you move someone from a chair with wheels, you lock the wheels so it doesn't roll away, and you get help if needed.

### Question 49

If the coach says 'move left a little,' you move left a little, not somewhere else.

### Question 50

A low step is easier and safer to climb than a high one.

### Question 51

You set the brakes on a rolling cart before you climb or lean on it, so it doesn't slide away.

### Question 52

To measure blood pressure right, sit like a student at a desk: feet flat, back straight, arm resting at chest height.

### Question 53

You knock before opening a bathroom door. The exam room is the same.

### Question 54

When helping someone, you focus on helping and being kind, not staring or rushing.

### Question 55

If a friend says 'call me Sam, not Samuel,' you call them Sam. Patients get the same courtesy.

### Question 56

You tell someone 'I'm going to help you sit up now' before you touch them, so they aren't surprised.

### Question 57

If you feel more comfortable with a certain person in the room, a good helper makes that happen.

### Question 58

You talk to people kindly and use words they understand, not big confusing words.

### Question 59

Some things are private, like a secret between friends. Health details are talked about in a quiet, private place.

### Question 60

If you have to stay in the room while someone changes, you look away to give them privacy.

### Question 61

When someone is nervous, you sit with them, give them a blanket, and tell them what will happen so it's less scary.

### Question 62

If someone says 'no thanks' to a blanket, you say 'okay' and leave it be.

### Question 63

If someone has been waiting a long time, you check on them and tell them what's going on.

### Question 64

We talk about 'a person who has something,' not 'that something person,' because the person comes first.

### Question 65

If the doctor steps out, you make sure the patient is covered and check if they need anything.

### Question 66

You close the curtain when you change so no one walking by can see in.

### Question 67

If someone feels shy, you listen, tell them how you'll keep things private, and go slowly.

### Question 68

You ask before helping and only help as much as needed, keeping the person covered.

### Question 69

You hold someone's hand when they step down so they don't trip. We do the same at the exam table.

### Question 70

You never leave someone wobbly alone on a high place; someone stays with them the whole time.

### Question 71

If something is too heavy to lift alone, you get a friend to help instead of trying alone.

### Question 72

You put a step stool on a flat, non-slippery floor and hold it steady while someone climbs.

### Question 73

Before you get out of a chair with wheels, you set the brake so it doesn't roll away.

### Question 74

If someone feels dizzy, they sit still and you stay with them and tell the doctor.

### Question 75

A wet, messy floor is like an ice rink or an obstacle course; people slip and trip.

### Question 76

A gait belt is like a helper's handhold that keeps someone steady while they walk or move.

### Question 77

If someone starts to tip over, you stay close and help them down gently, then shout for help.

### Question 78

If someone falls, first make sure they're safe and call for help; don't try to yank them up.

### Question 79

Someone who is unsteady on their feet and takes medicine that makes them dizzy is more likely to fall.

### Question 80

A cord across the floor is like a tripwire; people can fall over it.

### Question 81

To pick up a heavy box, you bend your knees and use your legs, not your back.

### Question 82

If someone can't catch their breath lying down, you tell the doctor right away and help them sit up.

### Question 83

If you need help, you ring a bell instead of climbing out alone and maybe falling.

### Question 84

You walk next to someone who uses a cane, at their speed, so you can help if they wobble.

### Question 85

Everyone helps keep patients from falling: spotting risks, lending a hand, keeping the floor safe, and telling the doctor.
